title: 'It started in Durban, not in PE' - de Villiers pushes back Australia's tampering timeline
excerpt: De Villiers was at the crease when the incident was caught on camera in the second Test
author: Cricbuzz Staff
body: AB de Villiers believes Australia's tampering of the ball during the 2018 series in South Africa started a Test earlier than recent accounts suggest - in the series opener at Durban rather than in Port Elizabeth.

The episode has been back in the news for a little over a fortnight, after Usman Khawaja's autobiography Sabr brought it up again. Since then, Khawaja, Chadd Sayers and Cameron Bancroft have each described in detail how sandpaper was used on the ball in the second Test at what is now Gqeberha, a match before Bancroft was caught on camera at Newlands.

De Villiers was closer to the action than most. He made a hundred against the reversing ball in Port Elizabeth, and he was at the crease in Cape Town when Bancroft was found with the sandpaper. He now says the problem goes back to the opening Test of the series.

"It started in Durban, by the way, not in PE," de Villiers said on his podcast. "And I'm very happy for people to quote me on that. We lost that first Test match in Durban with the ball reversing at a very, very interesting time. Way too early for anyone to reverse a ball at Kingsmead.

"Trust me, I've played a lot of cricket there. So whatever they did there, whether it was sandpaper or a nail or I don't care. I honestly do not care. The fact of the matter is they were caught and everyone knew.
"The bowlers in particular knew because the ball doesn't just reverse. It's not your first Test match for Australia. So just stand up and say, 'guys, we were wrong'."

That doesn't match Bancroft's account. In a long first-person piece published last week, the opener said Australia did not use sandpaper in Durban, a Test in which Mitchell Starc's reverse swing did much of the damage. He did, however, admit that other methods were in play.

"Casting forward to the first Test in Durban, sandpaper was not used," he wrote. "There were more traditional methods of maintaining the ball, including saliva. I cannot say with certainty whether mints or lollies were involved. Probably quarter-seam picking, this practice became so normal after my first Test.

"Importantly for the chronology of events, I was not responsible for the ball in that Test. However, what happened in the second Test in Port Elizabeth was different. It was a significant escalation. And it was where I became directly involved."

Australia had noticed how early the ball started moving at the time. Speaking after the opening day, when the visitors batted first, David Warner said, "We didn't assess for reverse [swing] in the first day - not after 24 or 25 overs."

For de Villiers, the recent focus on which tool was used misses the point entirely. "It's the weirdest thing because everyone's talking about the sandpaper now," he said. "That's the point everyone's missing at the moment. And it confuses me so much. Why are we all so worried about the object that was used? The fact of the matter is there was a premeditated decision made to do something illegal on the ground. And every single person knew about it. I've zero per cent doubt about it."
He was quick to admit that South Africa, and he himself, also looked for every advantage with the old ball. But he drew a firm line at what Australia did.

"I'm not playing all innocent and saying that I'm the perfect person," he said. "We all try and get the ball to reverse. We try and bounce it in. We try and do it in a legal manner and we try and push the boundaries as much as possible.

"So I'm not this beautiful angel trying to say that he's wrong and he's wrong and he's wrong. We all have tried over the years to get the ball to do something, to get an edge, but obviously not being as stupid as to take an object onto the field and blatantly cheating."
